components.text: The copper band is Chang'e-6's range: at the bottom of the near-side range, overlapping the Chang'e-5 estimate. The paper says “potentially drier”
“More reduced” means less oxygen was available when the magma formed

footnote: Source: He et al. (Nature, 2025), Zhang et al. (Nature Communications, 2025), Hu et al. (Nature, 2021)
notes: Exhibit six: looking through the basalt at the mantle beneath it. A team sieved 578 grains from 5 grams of Chang'e-6 soil and worked out that the mantle source of this far-side basalt held 1 to 1.5 micrograms of water per gram, at the very bottom of the range estimated from near-side samples. The paper's own wording is that the far-side mantle is potentially drier. Some reports said it was markedly drier than the near side, which goes too far: Chang'e-5 put the near-side mantle source at 1 to 5 micrograms per gram, so the two overlap. Another paper studied 23 Chang'e-6 basalt fragments and measured oxygen fugacity, a gauge of how much oxygen was available when the magma formed. The far side came out at minus 1.93, lower than the minus 0.80 for Apollo and Chang'e-5 basalts, which means more reduced. Taken together, the far-side mantle may differ from the near side, but each result still rests on samples from one place.
